Trump openly called on Carr to revoke licenses, stating on Air Force One in September 2025 that Carr is a patriot who would decide if networks should have their licenses taken away.

existing.description_long: On April 2, 2025, Trump staged a theatrical Rose Garden event he branded Liberation Day, unveiling sweeping reciprocal tariffs on virtually all U.S. trading partners — a 10% baseline on all imports, rising to 54% total on China (34% new plus existing 20%), 20% on EU goods, and country-specific rates reaching as high as 49% on Cambodia. The Dow plummeted 2,231 points on April 4. The VIX fear index surged 60% in under a week. Nike fell 14%, Apple lost $310 billion in market cap, Amazon shed $200 billion. JP Morgan warned of global recession if tariffs were sustained. Retirement accounts, pension funds, and ordinary investors absorbed catastrophic losses. Trump dismissed the carnage, claiming tariffs would make America wealthy again.

existing.description_long: Donald Trump signed an executive order dismantling Voice of America, the federally funded news organization established during World War II to counter Nazi propaganda, placing 1,300 journalists on administrative leave while accusing the globally respected broadcaster of being 'anti-Trump,' 'radical,' and 'leftist propaganda.' The order directed VOA managers to 'minimize performance to the least presence and function mandated by law' while stripping resources from an organization that reaches hundreds of millions globally with independent journalism. Trump's dismantlement targeted VOA's parent organization, the U.S. Agency for Global Media, which also funds Radio Free Europe, Radio Free Asia, and other outlets originally created to combat authoritarian propaganda from Iran, China, and Russia. VOA Director Mike Abramowitz warned that the destruction hindered the organization's 'crucial mission' at a time when U.S. adversaries were 'investing substantial resources in fabricating narratives that undermine the U.S.' The White House justified the destruction by claiming taxpayers should not fund 'radical propaganda,' despite VOA's charter requiring objective journalism and its role as America's primary tool for countering foreign disinformation. The dismantlement eliminated America's most important soft power asset for projecting democratic values globally, leaving the field open to Chinese and Russian state media while destroying decades of credibility built through independent reporting during the Cold War and beyond.

existing.title: 'I Could Shoot Somebody on Fifth Avenue' - Immunity Boasting
existing.description_short: 'I Could Shoot Somebody on Fifth Avenue' - Immunity Boasting
existing.description_long: During a campaign rally in Iowa on January 23, 2016, Donald Trump made one of his most revealing statements about the loyalty of his supporters, boasting: 'I could stand in the middle of Fifth Avenue and shoot somebody and I wouldn't lose voters.' The comment came during a discussion of his popularity with evangelical Christians, as Trump marveled at his ability to maintain support despite controversial statements. The 'Fifth Avenue' remark was initially dismissed as typical Trump hyperbole, but it proved to be prophetically accurate about his supporters' willingness to overlook any transgression. The statement revealed Trump's understanding that he had created a cult of personality so strong that even committing murder in broad daylight wouldn't shake his base's loyalty. More disturbingly, it showed his casual attitude toward violence and his belief in his own immunity from consequences. The comment became a touchstone for Trump's presidency, as his supporters indeed proved willing to defend him through every scandal, impeachment, and criminal indictment. The Fifth Avenue boast represented Trump's explicit acknowledgment that he had transcended normal political accountability, creating a movement based on personal devotion rather than policy or principle. Years later, as Trump faced multiple criminal indictments, his support among his base remained largely unchanged, proving his 2016 prediction horrifyingly accurate.

original_title: EPA Enforcement Collapses to Historic Low — Polluters Given Effective Immunity

existing.title: EPA Enforcement Collapses to Historic Low — Polluters Given Effective Immunity
existing.description_short: EPA Enforcement Collapses to Historic Low — Polluters Given Effective Immunity
existing.description_long: A comprehensive report by the Environmental Integrity Project, released in February 2026, documented that the Trump EPA brought only 16 civil lawsuits against polluters on behalf of the Department of Justice in all of 2025 — a figure 81% lower than the first year of Trump's own first term in 2017 (86 cases), 76% lower than Biden's first year (67 cases), and 87% lower than Obama's second-term first year. Superfund consent decrees hit a new low with just 7 in 2025 versus 31 in 2017; Clean Air Act consent decrees numbered only 1 versus 26 in 2017; and Clean Water Act consent decrees dropped to 4, a record low. EPA administrative monetary penalties against polluters totaled only $41 million through September 2025, down $8 million in real terms from Biden's first year. At least a third of DOJ's environmental enforcement attorneys left the department during 2025, gutting the pipeline of cases. In a December 5, 2025 internal memo, EPA's Office of Enforcement and Compliance Assurance outlined a new obstacle course requiring political clearance for enforcement actions, and reframed the agency's mission away from overzealous enforcement intended to cripple industry based on climate zealotry. EIP Executive Director Jen Duggan declared: Our nation's landmark environmental laws are meaningless when EPA does not enforce the rules.

existing.title: AI Deepfakes and Pro-Trump Bot Networks Flood 2026 Midterm Campaigns Without Federal Regulation
existing.description_short: AI Deepfakes and Pro-Trump Bot Networks Flood 2026 Midterm Campaigns Without Federal Regulation
existing.description_long: By early 2026, at least 15 campaign ads featuring AI-generated content had run in federal, state, and local races, with no federal law requiring disclosure or prohibition — the Trump administration made no effort to regulate the technology and Congress had failed to pass pending bills. The National Republican Senatorial Committee released an AI-generated video in March 2026 depicting Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico reading real tweets, with the fabricated video presented as if authentic. A Trump-aligned outside group, Citizens for Sanity, produced a deepfake of Talarico in a dress singing; AI attack ads ran in Kentucky, Georgia, Massachusetts, and Texas primaries. A Reuters investigation published March 28, 2026, found AI deepfakes were expected to spread with few guardrails and that Republicans are embracing AI to a greater extent than Democrats. The New York Times discovered hundreds of fake pro-Trump AI-generated influencer accounts on Instagram, TikTok, and Facebook in April 2026, part of what experts described as a pre-midterm push using avatars created in bulk at low cost by content farms. The complete absence of federal enforcement — with the FEC lacking a quorum and the DOJ focused on targeting perceived enemies — left voters with no protection against a tidal wave of AI-generated political disinformation in the most consequential election of Trump's second term.

original_title: OFCCP Ceases Affirmative Action Enforcement for Contractors

existing.title: OFCCP Ceases Affirmative Action Enforcement for Contractors
existing.description_short: OFCCP Ceases Affirmative Action Enforcement for Contractors
existing.description_long: On January 21, 2025, Trump's executive order revoking EO 11246 triggered an immediate halt to all affirmative action enforcement for federal contractors, a 60-year-old framework protecting millions of workers. The Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs (OFCCP), housed within the Department of Labor, was ordered to immediately cease and desist all investigative and enforcement activity tied to EO 11246. Acting Labor Secretary Vincent Micone issued a memo on January 24 directing the agency accordingly, administratively closing all approximately 2,000 pending compliance reviews that the Biden administration had scheduled for fiscal year 2025. Companies including Meta, Google, and Pfizer that had been slated for civil rights audits received formal closure notices. The Obama-era EO 13672 — which specifically prohibited federal contractors from discriminating on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity — was also revoked, eliminating protection for LGBTQ+ workers at companies doing business with the federal government, estimated to involve roughly 25 percent of the U.S. civilian workforce. Federal contractors were given a 90-day grace period until April 21, 2025 to wind down compliance with the old regulatory scheme. New contracts and grants were required to include certifications that recipients do not run DEI programs deemed discriminatory. Civil rights advocates called it the most significant rollback of workforce civil rights protections since the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

existing.title: DOJ Indicts NY AG Letitia James on Trumped-Up Fraud Charges
existing.description_short: DOJ Indicts NY AG Letitia James on Trumped-Up Fraud Charges
existing.description_long: Letitia James, the New York Attorney General who had won a landmark $454 million civil fraud judgment against Trump and his companies in 2022, became a primary target of DOJ retaliation in Trump's second term. In March 2025, FHFA Director Bill Pulte — a Trump ally — referred James to the DOJ alleging she had misrepresented information on a mortgage application. Despite a five-month investigation finding insufficient evidence to indict, Trump fired U.S. Attorney Erik Siebert in September 2025 specifically for refusing to bring charges against James and Comey. Ed Martin, Trump's special attorney and Weaponization Working Group director, sent James's attorney a letter saying he would take her resignation as an act of good faith even before any charges were filed. In October 2025, Lindsey Halligan — the same unlawfully appointed prosecutor who indicted Comey — secured a grand jury indictment against James on charges of bank fraud and making false statements. James pleaded not guilty and called the charges baseless and driven by political retribution. On November 24, 2025, the same judge who dismissed the Comey case dismissed James's indictment on the same grounds: Halligan's unlawful appointment. Subsequent federal grand juries in both Norfolk and Alexandria declined to re-indict James. The DOJ appealed. The mortgage fraud investigations of both James and Schiff were themselves investigated for potential DOJ misconduct.

existing.description_short: Election Lawyer Fundraising Scheme - Grifting 'Stop the Steal'
existing.description_long: Donald Trump and his legal team ran a massive fundraising scheme around their 'Stop the Steal' election fraud claims, raising over $250 million from supporters for legal challenges that were largely nonexistent or frivolous while pocketing most of the money for other purposes. The scheme involved sending hundreds of fundraising emails claiming donations would fund crucial legal battles to overturn the election, when in reality most of the money went to Trump's political action committee and other non-legal expenses. Small-dollar donors believing they were funding legitimate legal challenges instead subsidized Trump's post-presidency political operation and personal expenses. The fundraising appeals used increasingly desperate language about stolen elections and urgent deadlines, extracting money from supporters who trusted Trump's claims about widespread fraud. Many of the promised legal challenges never materialized, while those that were filed were quickly dismissed by courts for lack of evidence. The scheme exploited Trump's most loyal supporters, including elderly Americans and those on fixed incomes who made repeated small donations believing they were saving democracy. Internal Trump campaign communications revealed that officials knew many fraud claims were false but continued raising money off them anyway. The 'Stop the Steal' fundraising operation represented one of the largest political fundraising frauds in American history, converting election lies into personal profit while deceiving millions of Americans about the integrity of the democratic process.

original_title: EO Bans Federal Funding for Gender-Affirming Care for Minors

existing.title: EO Bans Federal Funding for Gender-Affirming Care for Minors
existing.description_short: EO Bans Federal Funding for Gender-Affirming Care for Minors
existing.description_long: On January 28, 2025, Trump signed Protecting Children from Chemical and Surgical Mutilation, an executive order declaring it federal policy not to fund, sponsor, promote, assist, or support the gender transition of anyone under 19. The order used medically contested terminology, labeling puberty blockers, hormones, and gender-affirming surgeries as chemical and surgical mutilation — language rejected by every major U.S. medical association including the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American Medical Association, and the American Psychological Association. It directed HHS to withdraw its 2022 guidance on gender-affirming care, directed the Defense Department to exclude such care from TRICARE coverage for military family dependents, and directed the Office of Personnel Management to exclude it from federal employee health benefit plans for families. It ordered agencies providing research or education grants to medical institutions to condition funding on ending gender-affirming care for minors. The Justice Department was directed to prioritize litigation and coordinate with states' attorneys general against so-called sanctuary states offering such care, and investigate hospitals for child abuse. Within weeks, hospitals in Virginia and other states that had been providing care paused services under pressure. Seventeen state attorneys general immediately signed a coalition letter opposing the order as scientifically wrong and unconstitutional. A federal judge in Seattle on March 1, 2025 issued a preliminary injunction blocking the funding restrictions in four states, ruling them unconstitutional.

The extensive preparation included 'challenging mock hearings,' 'intensive coaching from Republican senators,' and 'lengthy closed-door meetings' where Trump's allies compelled candidates to 'face their weaknesses, refine their messages, and practice avoiding potential pitfalls' while demonstrating 'unwavering loyalty to the president-elect.' The loyalty-focused training represented a dramatic departure from traditional Cabinet preparation, with increased expectation that nominees would 'exhibit a strong and clear commitment to the president-elect's agenda' rather than the independent judgment expected of constitutional officers. Mock hearing sessions included 'interruptions, heated exchanges among mock committee members, personal attacks, and other disruptive tactics' designed to test nominees' ability to maintain loyalty to Trump under pressure rather than defend constitutional principles or departmental missions. existing.description_long: The Committee to Protect Journalists reported in its April 2025 first-100-days assessment that requests for safety training, threat counseling, and emergency assistance from U.S.-based journalists had surged to historic levels — with CPJ providing safety training to more than 530 journalists in the United States between November 8, 2024 and March 7, 2025, compared to just 20 reporters trained throughout all of 2022. The CPJ noted a qualitative shift from Trump's first term: administration attacks were no longer vague enemy of the people rhetoric but direct, named targeting of specific outlets — AP, NPR, PBS, CBS, NBC, ABC — in their entirety. On World Press Freedom Day 2026, CPJ and Amnesty International USA jointly warned of relentless targeting of journalists, citing the arrest of Georgia Fort while covering an immigration protest, a pattern reminiscent of repressive government tactics CPJ has documented around the world. The U.S. fell dramatically in the Reporters Without Borders 2025 Press Freedom Index.

existing.title: Trump Permanently Expels AP from Air Force One and Presidential Pool Over Gulf of America Defiance
existing.description_short: Trump Permanently Expels AP from Air Force One and Presidential Pool Over Gulf of America Defiance
existing.description_long: On February 14, 2025, the White House formally barred Associated Press reporters and photographers from Air Force One and the Oval Office pool, an unprecedented punitive expulsion of the world's largest news wire service — which reaches an estimated 4 billion readers daily in 100 countries — solely because AP declined to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America in its global stylebook. Trump said publicly at Mar-a-Lago on February 18, We're going to keep them out until such time as they agree that it's the Gulf of America, framing a stylistic editorial decision as grounds for permanent exclusion from presidential coverage. AP photographers were physically blocked from the West Palm Beach airport tarmac to document Air Force One's arrival, and AP reporters were turned away from an Oval Office news conference with El Salvador President Nayib Bukele on April 14, 2025, in defiance of a court order by Judge Trevor McFadden issued just days earlier. The AP filed suit arguing First Amendment retaliation, and McFadden found the administration had likely violated free speech protections, but the White House appealed and continued its exclusions while the case moved through the courts. The White House simultaneously stripped the independent White House Correspondents' Association of its traditional role in selecting pool members, replacing it with administration-controlled access that Reuters, AP, and Bloomberg called a direct threat to the dissemination of reliable information about the presidency.

After massive public opposition and legal challenges, the Trump administration was forced to rescind the proposed regulations in July 2020, representing a major victory for First Amendment rights. The anti-protest scheme demonstrated Trump's authoritarian instincts to suppress dissent by making constitutional rights economically impossible for ordinary Americans to exercise.

The back-to-back bankruptcies severely damaged Trump's reputation among institutional lenders.

existing.description_short: DOGE Seeks Access to IRS Taxpayer Data on All Americans
existing.description_long: In February 2025, Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency sought access to the IRS's Integrated Data Retrieval System — a heavily protected database containing the financial records, tax returns, Social Security numbers, bank account details, and employment information of every taxpayer, business, and nonprofit in the country. DOGE software engineer Gavin Kliger was set to be granted access imminently, according to IRS sources. Democratic Senators Ron Wyden and Elizabeth Warren wrote to the acting IRS Commissioner calling the proposal weaponization of taxpayer data. The move came alongside DOGE already having penetrated Treasury Department payment systems, Social Security Administration records, and at least seven other major agency databases. A Washington Post investigation found DOGE had secured access to competitors' trade secrets and nonpublic regulatory data at those agencies. Privacy advocates warned the consolidation of data from multiple agencies in DOGE's hands had no legal precedent.

existing.description_long: On March 25, 2025, Trump signed EO 14248 Preserving and Protecting the Integrity of American Elections, which the Brennan Center called an illegal attempt to take control of major parts of the nation's election systems. The order unilaterally directed the independent Election Assistance Commission to require passport-level documentation for voter registration — a show-your-papers mandate that, since only about half of Americans hold passports, would disenfranchise millions disproportionately impacting people of color, young voters, and low-income Americans. The order also directed the EAC to decertify all voting machines in 39 states within 180 days and replace them with systems that did not yet exist on the market. It granted Elon Musk's DOGE access to sensitive voter registration files from all 50 states. A federal court permanently blocked the citizenship documentation provision on October 31, 2025, finding the president lacks constitutional authority to alter election procedures.

existing.description_long: Executive Order 14168, 'Defending Women from Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring Biological Truth to the Federal Government,' signed on January 20, 2025, directed every federal agency to remove all statements, policies, regulations, forms, and communications that 'promote or otherwise inculcate gender ideology.' A follow-up OPM memo dated January 29, 2025 set a 5 p.m. Friday deadline for agencies to strip gender ideology from websites, contracts, emails, and employee resource groups, and to place employees whose positions involved 'inculcating or promoting gender ideology' on paid administrative leave. By January 31 CDC webpages on HIV among transgender people, the Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System database, and HPV vaccination guidance had been removed. The order rescinded five prior executive orders and presidential memoranda dating to the Obama and Biden eras, including EO 13988 and EO 14075 on LGBTQ+ protections. The Census Bureau's sexual orientation and gender identity data page also went offline.

existing.title: Taj Mahal Collapses: Trump's First Bankruptcy and $675 Million Junk Bond Disaster
existing.description_short: Taj Mahal Collapses: Trump's First Bankruptcy and $675 Million Junk Bond Disaster
existing.description_long: On July 17, 1991, Trump Taj Mahal — billed as the world's largest casino at a construction cost of $1 billion — filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection just 15 months after its grand opening in April 1990. The casino had been financed with $675 million in junk bonds at a crushing 14 percent interest rate, a debt load so severe the property could not generate enough cash flow to service it even at peak revenues. As part of the reorganization plan, Trump surrendered 50 percent ownership of the casino to bondholders in exchange for a reduced interest rate of 11.35 percent. The bankruptcy was the first of six Trump entities to seek Chapter 11 protection over the following two decades, and exposed the fundamental hollowness of Trump's self-promoted image as a master dealmaker. Hundreds of small contractors and suppliers who had built and stocked the casino were paid cents on the dollar or nothing at all.

original_title: Hegseth's Signal Catastrophe: Defense Secretary Texts Classified Yemen War Plans to Journalist

existing.title: Hegseth's Signal Catastrophe: Defense Secretary Texts Classified Yemen War Plans to Journalist
existing.description_short: Hegseth's Signal Catastrophe: Defense Secretary Texts Classified Yemen War Plans to Journalist
existing.description_long: On March 13, 2025, national security adviser Mike Waltz accidentally added Atlantic editor-in-chief Jeffrey Goldberg to an encrypted Signal group chat called Houthi PC small group, which included Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Vice President JD Vance, CIA Director John Ratcliffe, and other senior officials. At 11:44 a.m. on March 15, Hegseth texted the group exact timings of warplane launches, weapons packages, and bomb drop schedules for imminent strikes on Houthi targets in Yemen — two hours before pilots were airborne. The Atlantic published the account on March 24, and on March 26 released the full Signal transcript, confirming that Hegseth had shared what current and former U.S. officials described as information that would have been classified. Trump initially claimed to know nothing about it; Hegseth falsely declared nobody was texting war plans. Democrats demanded investigations, calling the use of a commercial app for operational military information a potential Espionage Act violation. No one was fired or criminally referred, and the White House declared the matter closed within days.

The policy explicitly targeted pride and Black Lives Matter flags that had flown at Biden-era embassies, including the U.S. Embassy in Nassau during Pride Month 2021 and U.S. facilities in Brazil. Pride flags had first been permitted at U.S. embassies under the Obama administration and were banned during Trump's first term starting in 2019.

Smith's two-volume report detailed how Trump stored documents related to nuclear programs, defense capabilities, foreign intelligence, and potential military vulnerabilities at his private club, which hosted hundreds of paying members and foreign nationals. Trump had been indicted on 37 federal counts before Cannon dismissed the case in 2024 on the grounds that Smith was not lawfully appointed. The documents — over 300 records with classified markings — included material on nuclear weapons programs and signals intelligence so sensitive that their compromise could cause irreplaceable loss of technical or human access that took years and significant resources to develop. In the second term, rather than implementing stronger security protocols at Mar-a-Lago, Trump continued using the club as a de facto second White House, and no damage assessment was ever publicly released.

existing.description_short: SAVE Program Weaponized to Flag 67 Million Voter Registrations as Suspect
existing.description_long: By May 2026, the Trump administration had run at least 67 million voter registrations — primarily from Republican-controlled states that agreed to share data — through a dramatically expanded version of the DHS Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) program. Originally designed to verify immigration status for benefits programs, SAVE was overhauled in spring 2025 to enable bulk scanning of state voter rolls against federal citizenship databases. The expanded system flagged tens of thousands of registrations as potential noncitizens or deceased persons, with some states then suspending those voters' eligibility with as little as 30 days to respond. A federal judge blocked the modified SAVE tool in June 2026. Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said DHS told her it planned to retain all uploaded state voter data for 10 years for audit purposes, raising concerns about a de facto federal voter database built through the backdoor.

original_title: EEOC Halts LGBTQ Discrimination Cases, Drops Trans Lawsuits

existing.title: EEOC Halts LGBTQ Discrimination Cases, Drops Trans Lawsuits
existing.description_short: EEOC Halts LGBTQ Discrimination Cases, Drops Trans Lawsuits
existing.description_long: Within days of Trump's inauguration, Acting EEOC Chair Andrea Lucas — appointed January 20, 2025 — ordered agency employees to halt processing of all sexual orientation and gender identity discrimination claims under Title VII, and Trump controversially dismissed two Democratic EEOC commissioners whose terms had not expired. In April 2025, the EEOC held an internal meeting directing intake staff to code all new gender-identity discrimination charges as 'C,' the lowest priority category reserved for meritless charges, effectively placing them on indefinite hold. Lucas dropped multiple pending EEOC lawsuits on behalf of transgender workers, rescinded Biden-era EEOC workplace harassment guidance on pronouns and bathroom access, and halted payments to state and local civil rights agencies for investigating gender identity cases. In July 2025, legal groups filed suit against the EEOC alleging it was unlawfully refusing to enforce federal workplace protections for transgender workers, citing Bostock v. Clayton County. Lucas acknowledged at a June 18 Senate confirmation hearing that transgender workers are legally protected under civil rights law but defended her decision to sideline their cases, saying the EEOC must comply with Trump's executive orders.

original_title: Trump Falsely Claims $88 Billion in Tariff Revenue in Two Months

existing.title: Trump Falsely Claims $88 Billion in Tariff Revenue in Two Months
existing.description_short: Trump Falsely Claims $88 Billion in Tariff Revenue in Two Months
existing.description_long: On June 11, 2025, President Trump told reporters at the Kennedy Center that the U.S. had brought in $88 billion in tariffs in two months, far beyond what anybody expected. He repeated the claim the following day at a White House bill signing. FactCheck.org investigation found the claim false: actual tariff revenue from the entire October 2024–May 2025 fiscal year totaled $81.4 billion — a period that included over three months when Biden was still president. No two-month period came close to $88 billion. Trump also claimed he had attracted $9 trillion in new U.S. investments — a figure the White House's own webpage listed as $5 trillion as of April 29, and $9.6 trillion by December 10. Economists noted the list included unverified pledges and pre-existing Biden-era investments recategorized under Trump. CBS News confirmed several listed investments had been announced before Trump's reelection. In a December 9 rally, Trump had inflated the investment total to $18 trillion, more than double the White House's own tally. Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell cited tariff uncertainty and forecast meaningful inflation increases. Trump responded by questioning whether Powell was a Democrat.

Corn, cotton, sorghum, wheat, and cattle producers were all affected. Trump announced a $12 billion farm bailout in December 2025 — effectively asking taxpayers to pay for his trade war's agricultural damage — following the $25.7 billion bailout during his first-term trade war.

original_title: EPA Dismantled: 23% Workforce Cut, Research Office Eliminated, Enforcement Gutted

existing.title: EPA Dismantled: 23% Workforce Cut, Research Office Eliminated, Enforcement Gutted
existing.description_short: EPA Dismantled: 23% Workforce Cut, Research Office Eliminated, Enforcement Gutted
existing.description_long: On July 18, 2025, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced the agency was eliminating its Office of Research and Development — the scientific backbone of EPA for over five decades, with roughly 1,500 scientists — and cutting the agency's total workforce by at least 23%, from 16,155 employees in January to 12,448, the smallest EPA headcount since the mid-1980s. The restructuring, Zeldin claimed, would save $748.8 million, but critics described it as the dismantling of the agency's scientific credibility. The first wave of cuts had begun February 14, 2025, when 388 probationary employees were terminated; by March 2025 additional layoffs were accelerating. Zeldin announced on March 12, 2025 what he called the greatest day of deregulation in U.S. history, proposing to roll back more than 30 environmental rules simultaneously, including reconsideration of the 2009 Endangerment Finding that underpins virtually all EPA climate regulation. Justin Chen, president of EPA's largest union, called the cuts devastating, citing the dismantling of research labs across the country. An independent report released in February 2026 found that EPA brought only 16 lawsuits against polluters in all of 2025, an 81% decline from Trump's own first term and a historic low.

existing.description_long: On May 2, 2025, Reporters Without Borders (RSF) published its 2025 World Press Freedom Index, ranking the United States 57th out of 180 countries — a drop of two additional places from its 2024 ranking, extending a slide of over 25 places in recent years. The U.S. now ranked one position behind Sierra Leone and was downgraded from satisfactory to problematic in press freedom status. RSF stated that Donald Trump's second term as president has led to an alarming deterioration in press freedom, indicative of an authoritarian shift in government. The economic indicator for U.S. press freedom had fallen more than 14 points in two years. Over 60 percent of journalists surveyed in Arizona, Florida, Nevada, and Pennsylvania said it was difficult to earn a living wage as a journalist, and 75 percent said their outlet struggles for economic viability. The U.S. Press Freedom Tracker recorded more than 170 attacks on journalists in 2025 — nearly double the previous year — driven by increased violence at protests and law enforcement confrontations. RSF cited Trump's efforts to censor government data, dismantle public broadcasters, weaponize regulatory agencies, halt international media freedom aid, and sue disfavored outlets as the primary drivers of the decline.

original_title: Congress Defunds Corporation for Public Broadcasting, CPB Shuts Down

existing.title: Congress Defunds Corporation for Public Broadcasting, CPB Shuts Down
existing.description_short: Congress Defunds Corporation for Public Broadcasting, CPB Shuts Down
existing.description_long: In May 2025, Trump signed an executive order directing the Corporation for Public Broadcasting to cease all direct and indirect funding to NPR and PBS, calling their journalism biased and not fair. On July 24, 2025, Trump signed a $9 billion rescissions bill that clawed back $1.1 billion in congressionally appropriated CPB funding through fiscal year 2027. CPB, which had channeled federal money to over 1,500 local public radio and television stations nationwide for nearly 60 years, announced on August 1, 2025 that it was beginning to wind down operations. CPB President Patricia Harrison called it the first time in nearly six decades Congress had refused to fund the corporation. NPR, PBS, and their more than 1,500 member stations — many serving rural communities with no commercial news alternatives — faced devastating funding gaps. The FCC simultaneously investigated NPR and PBS for alleged commercialization violations under Chairman Carr. Approximately 50 million Americans already lived in news deserts in 2025 according to the Medill Local News Initiative. NPR pledged $8 million from its budget to help local stations. The shutdown represented the most comprehensive government elimination of public broadcasting infrastructure in U.S. history, undertaken as critics argued it was designed to silence journalism hostile to the administration.

existing.description_long: On January 20, 2025, Trump's first day in office, he signed Executive Order 14168, Defending Women from Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring Biological Truth to the Federal Government. The sweeping order declared U.S. federal policy would recognize only two sexes — male and female — and ordered all government agencies to purge any language recognizing gender identity. It directed the State Department to restrict passports and visas to only reflect sex assigned at birth, eliminating the Biden-era X gender marker and self-identification option. It ordered the Bureau of Prisons to halt all gender-affirming medical care for incarcerated transgender people and to house them according to birth sex. Clayton County so it would not protect gender identity in federal programs, reversing the legal basis for transgender civil rights across government. It directed agencies to remove all statements, policies, and forms acknowledging gender identity, and prohibited federal funds from being used to promote gender ideology. The White House Gender Policy Council was dissolved. Critics including the ACLU and Lambda Legal immediately challenged portions of the order as unconstitutional, arguing it codified discrimination against a vulnerable minority.

existing.description_long: On March 27, 2025, AP chief Washington photographer Evan Vucci testified under oath in federal court about the professional and constitutional damage caused by the Trump White House's ban on AP photojournalists. Vucci, who had photographed every major presidential moment for over a decade including the iconic 2024 Butler, Pennsylvania assassination attempt image, testified that the ban left AP really struggling to keep up with competitors at defining news events of the early Trump second term. It's hurting us big time. We're basically dead in the water on major news stories, Vucci stated. AP chief White House correspondent Zeke Miller also testified to the access restrictions' impact. AP photojournalists had been blocked from Air Force One, the Oval Office, and pool events continuously since February 11, 2025. An AP photographer was additionally barred from the West Palm Beach airport tarmac to document Air Force One's arrival. Despite a court injunction on April 8 ordering access restored, the White House again barred AP from an Oval Office event on April 14. The targeting of photojournalists — who document the visual record of the presidency — represented a specific attack on the visual historical archive of American democracy, motivated solely by the AP's refusal to rename the Gulf of Mexico in its style guide.

The dual memecoin launches scandalized presidential ethics experts who noted the incoming president was using his inauguration to pump speculative crypto assets in which he held a dominant financial interest.

CPJ's Katherine Jacobson said Trump's 'flurry of executive actions' created 'a real chilling effect and have the potential to curtail media freedoms' through access restrictions, FCC investigations of major networks, and systematic attacks on press credibility. The dramatic decline reflected Trump's systematic campaign against media freedom, including calling journalists 'enemy of the people,' celebrating reporter injuries, and using government power to investigate news outlets that criticized him. International press freedom organizations warned that the U.S. was losing its status as a global leader in press freedom while providing a model for authoritarian leaders worldwide to justify their own media crackdowns.

The wall construction enriched Trump donors and allies who received no-bid contracts, including companies with no prior experience building border barriers. Trump repeatedly lied about the wall's progress, claiming he had 'completed' or 'finished' the wall when only 47 miles of new barriers were built in previously unwalled areas. The wall project epitomized Trump's corruption: stealing taxpayer money for a politically motivated vanity project that enriched his allies while failing to achieve its stated purpose.

original_title: Trump Blames Newsom for Sabotaging California Wildfires With Fake Water Restoration Declaration

existing.title: Trump Blames Newsom for Sabotaging California Wildfires With Fake Water Restoration Declaration
existing.description_short: Trump Blames Newsom for Sabotaging California Wildfires With Fake Water Restoration Declaration
existing.description_long: As catastrophic wildfires devastated the Los Angeles area beginning January 7, 2025 — killing at least 10 people, forcing 180,000 evacuations, and destroying more than 10,000 structures — President-elect Donald Trump immediately launched a disinformation campaign blaming California Governor Gavin Newsom for deliberately causing the disaster. On January 8, 2025, Trump posted to Truth Social that Newsom refused to sign the water restoration declaration put before him that would have allowed millions of gallons of water to flow daily into many parts of California — a document that state officials confirmed does not exist, with Newsom's office calling it pure fiction. Trump claimed hydrants ran dry because Newsom diverted water to protect an essentially worthless fish called a smelt — a claim water policy experts called physically impossible, since Los Angeles receives its water primarily from the Colorado River and Owens Valley, not the Sacramento Delta; Peter Gleick of the Pacific Institute called the framing nothing short of irresponsible. Trump also falsely claimed there was NO MONEY IN FEMA when Congress had appropriated $29 billion specifically for FEMA's Disaster Relief Fund just weeks earlier. The conspiracy narrative included additional false claims that a billionaire couple was hoarding water and that firefighters had used women's handbags rather than proper equipment; online posts falsely attributed the fires to arson by MAGA-affiliated groups, fabricating police searches for persons of interest.

existing.description_short: ICE Arrests Parishioner on Catholic Church Grounds in Inland Empire
existing.description_long: On June 20, 2025 — World Refugee Day — federal immigration agents conducted enforcement operations on the grounds of two Catholic churches in San Bernardino County, California, marking a stark application of Trump's January 21 order eliminating protections for sensitive locations. At Our Lady of Lourdes Church in Montclair, agents detained a longtime parishioner who was doing landscaping work on church property. According to the Roman Catholic Diocese of San Bernardino, the man was a parishioner whose family was involved in the church ministry. In a separate incident the same day, agents chased several men onto the parking lot of St. Adelaide Parish in Highland. DHS Assistant Secretary Tricia McLaughlin disputed characterizations of the events. Bishop Alberto Rojas of the Diocese of San Bernardino wrote to parishioners that authorities are now seizing brothers and sisters indiscriminately, without respect for their right to due process and their dignity as children of God, calling the raids not of the Gospel of Jesus Christ. The newly appointed Bishop of the Diocese of San Diego, Michael Pham — himself a Vietnamese refugee who came to the US in 1981 — joined clergy outside the San Diego federal building the same day to witness immigration proceedings. Six California Republican state legislators signed a letter asking Trump to focus only on violent criminals, saying ICE raids at farms, churches, and workplaces were harming the communities we represent.

The executive order attempted to sidestep the Supreme Court precedent by directing prosecution for 'related crimes' during flag burning incidents, while threatening visa revocation and deportation for foreign nationals who engage in the protected political expression. Free speech organizations called the order a dangerous precedent that could lead to criminalizing other forms of political protest, with Trump's defiance of established constitutional law representing an authoritarian rejection of judicial authority over executive power.

original_title: DOJ Vacates Oath Keepers and Proud Boys Seditious Conspiracy Convictions

existing.title: DOJ Vacates Oath Keepers and Proud Boys Seditious Conspiracy Convictions
existing.description_short: DOJ Vacates Oath Keepers and Proud Boys Seditious Conspiracy Convictions
existing.description_long: In April 2026, the Trump DOJ moved to vacate the convictions of Oath Keepers founder Stewart Rhodes and other seditious conspiracy defendants who had received sentence commutations but not pardons in January 2025. This reversed the Biden-era DOJ's landmark victories in the largest and most serious prosecutions stemming from January 6. U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta, who had overseen the trials, reluctantly granted the motion but wrote a stinging rebuke, stating the government asks to absolve these Defendants of crimes against the United States itself without alleging insufficient evidence or prosecutorial misconduct. In July 2026, Judge Timothy Kelly similarly dismissed the seditious conspiracy cases against Proud Boys leaders Ethan Nordean, Joseph Biggs, Zachary Rehl, and Dominic Pezzola, writing no one should mistake the Court's granting of the Government's motion for its agreement with those decisions and calling January 6 a perilous event and an attack on a coordinate branch of government. On August 5, 2026, Mehta dismissed the final Oath Keepers indictment, writing: This is the last of the prosecutions seeking to hold accountable those responsible for the events of Jan. 6. That book is now closed... Today's epilogue diminishes the gravity of that day, denigrates the work of the prosecutors and law enforcement officers who secured these convictions, and excuses criminal acts that caused a centuries-long pillar of our democracy — the peaceful transfer of presidential power — to buckle. The court cannot write a different ending.

original_title: Trump's Ukraine $350 Billion Hoax — Doubling the Real Aid Figure to Paint NATO as America's Con Artist

existing.title: Trump's Ukraine $350 Billion Hoax — Doubling the Real Aid Figure to Paint NATO as America's Con Artist
existing.description_short: Trump's Ukraine $350 Billion Hoax — Doubling the Real Aid Figure to Paint NATO as America's Con Artist
existing.description_long: From February 2025 onward, President Trump repeatedly and falsely claimed the United States had spent $350 billion supporting Ukraine's war against Russia, using the inflated figure to demand Ukraine repay the debt through a mineral extraction deal he pegged at $1 trillion and to portray NATO allies as freeloaders draining American taxpayers. The actual U.S. figure, according to Trump's own government, was approximately $183 billion in total appropriations — with only $83 billion actually disbursed as of December 2024 — and the Kiel Institute for the World Economy calculated the U.S. total at $119 billion; European nations had collectively provided approximately $138 billion, meaning Europe outspent the U.S. contrary to Trump's claims. Trump made the false $350 billion claim during his meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on February 28, 2025 — telling him we gave you $350 billion for military equipment — and repeated it in a March 4, 2025 address to Congress; Trump's own State Department issued a statement the same day that contradicted the figure. Trump also falsely claimed Ukraine started the war with Russia by refusing to make a deal — Russia launched its full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022 — and called Zelenskyy a dictator without elections, misleadingly ignoring that Ukrainian law requires suspension of elections during martial law. These false claims provided the rhetorical scaffolding for Trump's decision to freeze military aid to Ukraine and leverage the conflict as a conspiracy against American interests.

existing.description_short: Birthright Citizenship Executive Order Blocked by Four Courts
existing.description_long: On January 20, 2025, his first day back in office, Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to refuse to recognize U.S. citizenship for children born on U.S. soil who do not have at least one parent who is a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident — a direct challenge to the 14th Amendment's birthright citizenship clause, in place since 1868. Three federal district judges immediately halted the order nationwide. The Supreme Court's June 27, 2025 ruling in the birthright citizenship litigation limited judges' power to issue universal injunctions in a 6-3 decision, but did not rule on the merits. The 9th Circuit on July 23, 2025 became the first appeals court to rule on the merits, holding Trump's order unconstitutional 2-1. The order, if ever enforced, would affect an estimated 150,000 babies born annually in the U.S. Legal scholars across the political spectrum noted the order attempts to rewrite constitutional text by executive fiat.

existing.title: Jermaine Thomas, Born on US Army Base in Germany, Deported to Jamaica He'd Never Visited
existing.description_short: Jermaine Thomas, Born on US Army Base in Germany, Deported to Jamaica He'd Never Visited
existing.description_long: In late May 2025, Jermaine Thomas, 39, was shackled at the wrists and ankles and placed on a flight to Kingston, Jamaica — a country he had never been to in his life. Thomas was born in 1986 at a US military hospital in Germany, where his father — a US citizen — was deployed as an Army soldier. His case had reached the US Supreme Court ten years earlier in a dispute over whether children born to US citizen servicemembers on overseas deployments should automatically receive citizenship. The court ruled against him. Thomas had no citizenship anywhere: not the United States (despite his father's decades of military service), not Germany (where he was born), not Jamaica (his father's ancestral homeland), and not Kenya (his mother's birthplace). When reached by CNN, Thomas described himself as legally stateless, calling from a homeless shelter in Kingston. He had no passport, no support network, and no connection to the country. DHS issued a statement calling him a violent, criminal illegal alien from Jamaica and describing Jamaica as his home country — a characterization the Austin Chronicle challenged in direct correspondence with the department, asking in what sense Jamaica was his home country. DHS did not respond. Thomas's case illustrates how the Trump administration's deportation framework was being applied even to people abandoned by the citizenship system because of technical legal gaps — leaving a man stateless on the basis of his father's military service.

The systematic forfeiture expansion represented Trump's support for law enforcement revenue generation through property seizure that disproportionately targeted low-income communities and minorities who lacked resources to challenge seizures in court, effectively creating taxation through confiscation that operated outside constitutional protections and due process requirements. The civil forfeiture program violated due process principles by allowing police to seize property based on suspicion rather than conviction, while creating financial incentives that corrupted law enforcement priorities by encouraging property seizure for profit rather than crime prevention and public safety protection. Trump's forfeiture expansion enabled what civil liberties advocates called 'legal theft' where police departments could fund special projects and equipment purchases through seized property while property owners faced expensive legal challenges to recover their belongings, creating system where seizure was easier than recovery regardless of innocence. The asset forfeiture system generated over $33 million annually for New York City Police Department alone, while Chicago Police Department received over $8 million in 2021, demonstrating massive scale of property seizure that operated as parallel funding mechanism for law enforcement agencies seeking to avoid legislative budget oversight. The forfeiture expansion represented implementation of Project 2025's law enforcement priorities that emphasized police power and resource generation over constitutional protections, transforming civil asset forfeiture from limited tool for major criminal investigations into widespread property seizure system that enabled police departments to self-fund through confiscation rather than democratic budget processes.

existing.title: Violence Against Women Act Defunding - Domestic Violence Support Elimination
existing.description_short: Violence Against Women Act Defunding - Domestic Violence Support Elimination
existing.description_long: Donald Trump systematically eliminated Violence Against Women Act funding by terminating grants for domestic violence shelters, sexual assault programs, and legal assistance while conducting 'partisan political' defunding of organizations that provided essential services to abuse survivors, creating what advocates called 'tremendous risks for survivors and their families' through systematic abandonment of violence prevention and support systems. The comprehensive VAWA destruction represented Trump's elimination of federal commitment to ending gender-based violence, cutting funding for programs that had provided hotlines, forensic nurse examiners, rape kits, crisis counselors, housing assistance, legal help, and medical care to survivors while claiming these services were not 'aligned with administration priorities.' The domestic violence defunding included eliminating support for LGBTQ+ and immigrant survivors who faced additional barriers while losing access to specialized programs, case management, counseling, and legal assistance that had enabled economic security and safety for people fleeing abusive relationships and sexual violence. Trump's VAWA targeting violated federal obligations to protect vulnerable populations by removing funding for programs proven to 'prevent and reduce violence' while increasing risks for survivors who lost access to essential services including protective orders, child custody assistance, and economic support that enabled independence from abusive partners. The violence prevention elimination created what legal experts called systematic abandonment where 'individuals are left on their own to deal with crippling assaults, their mental, physical, and emotional damage be damned' while communities lost resources that had historically reduced domestic violence and sexual assault through prevention education and survivor support. The VAWA defunding represented Project 2025's vision of violence response based on individual responsibility rather than community support, eliminating federal programs that had saved lives while forcing survivors to navigate abuse without the legal, economic, and social assistance that had historically enabled safety and recovery from gender-based violence.
